title: The Orthodox revival
hookLine: after communism, churches rebuilt across Eastern Europe

lines: A SWIMMING POOL WHERE THE ALTAR WAS.
BUILT AGAIN ON THE SAME SPOT.
cards: In the middle of Moscow there was once a great white cathedral with golden domes. Under Stalin's government it was blown up.
For years the site held a hole in the ground, and then an open-air swimming pool, steaming in the winter cold. People swam laps where the altar had been.
Then the government that built the pool was gone, and the cathedral was rebuilt on the same spot, dome by dome.

teach.b: That cathedral is one story among smaller ones like it.
Across Russia, Ukraine, Romania, Bulgaria, Georgia and their neighbors, communist governments had closed churches, or turned them into warehouses, museums, cinemas, even stables.
When those governments fell, the churches came back.

teach.h: BELLS RECAST, ICONS OUT OF HIDING.
teach.b: Bells were recast. Icons came out of hiding. Monasteries that had stood empty took in monks and nuns again.
Grown adults lined up to be baptized. The Bible has a scene that sounds like this.

When exiles came home to Jerusalem, the book of Ezra says, they laid the foundation of a new temple, and the old men who remembered the first one wept with a loud voice, "and many shouted aloud for joy."

teach.h: THE SHOUT OF JOY AND THE WEEPING.
teach.b: Then, in the King James Bible: "the people could not discern the noise of the shout of joy from the noise of the weeping of the people."
That's what rebuilding sounds like: joy and grief so mixed you can't pull them apart. Rebuilding stirs questions too.

People inside and outside these churches have argued about how close a rebuilt church should stand to a government, and Orthodox Christians themselves hold different views on it. Walls can be raised with money and stone.
Teaching a generation that had never been inside how to stand before an icon, light a candle and pray takes longer.

teach.h: LET US RISE UP AND BUILD.
teach.b: In Nehemiah, the people look at the ruined walls and say, "Let us rise up and build."

how: In Orthodox churches, worshipers usually stand, light candles before icons, kiss them and cross themselves, and the Divine Liturgy is sung, often with no instruments, across Russia, Ukraine, Romania, Greece, Georgia and beyond.

games.q: the foundation of the new temple is laid in Jerusalem. you're an old man who saw the first temple standing. what do you do?
o: shout for joy with everyone else.
games.why: Ezra says the old men wept with a loud voice while many shouted for joy, and no one could tell the two sounds apart.

practice: Picture stepping inside an Orthodox church: a heavy door, the smell of beeswax and incense, few pews or none, people standing before a wall of icons, Christ, Mary and the saints, lit by thin candles in a tray of sand.
Someone old lights a candle and crosses herself; someone young watches how she does it. If you pray, pray there for the churches that were rebuilt; if not, simply stand and look.

wordCard.voice: Nehemiah. The Old Testament book about rebuilding Jerusalem's walls after exile, echoed in Eastern Europe's rebuilt cathedrals, bells recast and icons returned after communism.
